gamma_ray.fact_ray: 25 facts: 25 π Moderate. Each is written beside its evidence above.
gamma_ray.built_from: JetBrains' own public documentation for Junie, its blog, legal and AI terms pages, the JetBrains Marketplace, and Junie's published llms

configs.what: Junie in a JetBrains IDE or the CLI with its defaults: sensitive actions ask first.
Commands the user allows run without asking.
A safety classifier approves terminal commands it considers safe.
Potentially sensitive actions run without approval.
The user or project configures MCP servers.
Junie runs on the customer's GitHub runners with the documented workflow permissions.
An AGENTS.md guidelines file; hooks in the early access CLI.

facts.label: It works across several domains or systems
facts.fact: The release post says Junie connects to databases configured in the IDE through DataGrip and the JetBrains Database plugin and works on SQL in the same session as the code.
facts.quote: writes, fixes, and validates SQL in the same session that handles your code

facts.label: The agent works independently; the person approves critical decisions only
facts.fact: In brave mode Auto, a safety check approves commands it classes as safe and asks for the rest.
facts.quote: automatically approves the ones it considers safe, while still asking for approval

facts.label: The agent has full autonomy within boundaries; the person monitors
facts.fact: With brave mode On, Junie CLI runs every sensitive action without asking; the user turns it on.
facts.quote: Junie CLI executes all potentially sensitive actions without user approval.

facts.label: It connects to external tools or services across a trust boundary
facts.fact: Junie CLI can connect to external tools through MCP servers that the user configures.
facts.quote: You can connect Junie CLI to external tools via Model Context Protocol (MCP).

facts.label: High-impact actions need a person's approval
facts.fact: Most terminal commands, edits outside the project and MCP tool calls wait for the user's approval.
facts.quote: Junie CLI will ask for approval from the user

facts.label: What it can reach is enumerated: scopes, permissions, tools
facts.fact: The Action Allowlist page documents a list of five action types (fileEditing, executables, mcpTools, readOutsideProject, readSecretFile), each taking allow or ask rules in the user's allowlist file; this is a documented list, not a measured grant.
facts.quote: There are five types of actions that can be allowed with the

facts.label: It asks for narrower access than the whole account
facts.fact: The page gives a junie.yaml template that the user copies into the repository's .github/workflows/; its job permissions block has three entries, contents, pull-requests and issues, each set to write.
facts.quote: permissions: contents: write pull-requests: write issues: write

facts.label: Test or evaluation results are published
facts.fact: The release post reports Junie's SWE-Rebench result (61.6% resolved) in a quote attributed to a Research Lead at Nebius, and links the SWE-Rebench site.

facts.label: There is a channel to report problems with it or contest its output
facts.fact: A /feedback command sends feedback on the current session, with its logs, to the Junie team.
facts.quote: Share feedback about the current session with the Junie team.

facts.label: It is machine-readable for agents: it publishes an llms.txt, an AGENTS.md, an API description or an agent card
facts.fact: junie.jetbrains.com serves an llms.txt and links an OpenAPI description; both resolved when fetched on 10 November 2026.

help.label: Our hypothesis, not their claim. Built from public pages only; nothing of theirs was tested.
help.pitch: RiskMandate would measure, for one real deployment of JetBrains's agents, what each agent was asked to do (its mandate), what its credentials and connections actually let it reach (its grant), and the difference between the two (the gap), and keep that as a written record. It is read-only: never in the request path.
